MCC MegaCell Compiler User Guide

Chapter 2

Running MCC

Setup

If you have an MCC license (max_mcc), you need to enable the MCC menu commands with the command mc_init. Typically, you add this command to the system .maxrc file ($MMI_TOOLS/../mmi_local/max/.maxrc) so everyone has access to it. If only specific users run MCC, they can add it to their own .maxrc files (~/mmi_private/max/.maxrc).

The mc_init command adds the MCC commands to the Tool menu in the MAX Layout Editor. All of the MCC commands are prefixed by the string MC for clarity. These commands are discussed in the next section. When a user attempts to execute any one of these commands, MAX checks that a valid MCC license is available, and if so, checks out that license for the remainder of the MAX session. Note that the mc_init command by itself does not check out an MCC license.

Running MCC

MCC provides four basic commands to MAX:

  • MC Build
    •

  • MC Netlist
    •

  • MC Critical Path
    •

  • MC What
    •

You can also run these commands in batch mode or by scripts. For more information concerning their syntax, see Running MCC in Batch Mode .

MC Build

The MC Build command tells MCC to build a megacell. It first prompts you with a popup that lets you choose the name of the megacell to create (see Figure 1). This megacell must be defined and loaded into MAX through the control program described in the Creating Megacells chapter. You can set the default megacell name by setting the following variable in the control program: 

      set MC(default_generator) <name>

If you were working on an SRAM, you might add the following line so you wouldn't have to enter it in the menu every time you restart MAX: 

      set MC(default_generator) sram

The popup form also allows you to turn off Via Programming and Port Propagation . Typically these should be turned on to create a complete megacell. However, when debugging a megacell, you might want to turn off one or the other to speed up the megacell generation.

    Figure 1: MC Build Popup Form 
     

Once you click on Done, a second popup form appears (see Figure 2) which provides more options specific to this megacell. The top of this form contains a list of any parameters and their default values. You can change these values to create a different version of this megacell or change the defaults in the control program. For a description of how to set up these defaults, see the section on Parameters .

    Figure 2: SRAM MegaCell Popup Form 
     

The bottom half of the menu (below the horizontal line) provides three different fields: prefix, suffix, and name. When MCC Build creates a megacell, it typically creates a number of hierarchical cells. Depending on the input parameters, these cells probably contain different numbers of leaf cells or other hierarchical cells and thus need unique names.

For example, if you need two types of SRAMs on your chip, one that has 128 rows and another that has 256 rows, the memory cores and spine are different between the two memories. The prefix and suffix fields allow you to add a prefix and suffix to all created cells. The suffix defaults to the concatenation of all of the parameter values, separated by underscores. If you had the one parameter, ROWS, the hierarchical cells memory_core and spine would be named by default: 

      memory_core_256, spine_256 
     

for the case where ROWS=256 and 

      memory_core_128, spine_128 
     

for the case where ROWS=128.

In addition to the suffix, you might want to prefix all generated cells by a unique ID. This might be either the name of your company or the section of the chip that this megacell goes into. To add a unique ID, simply change the prefix field. For example, if these two previously described memories went into the instruction unit of the chip, you might set the prefix to be "IU_" and then the cells would be named: 

      IU_memory_core_256, IU_spine_256, etc. 
     

Lastly, the top level cell of the megacell sometimes requires a special name, like ASYNC_RAM128X10, or something similar, which doesn't fit with the prefix and suffix naming scheme. The name field allows you to name this cell specially.

As described previously, if a suffix is not specified, it defaults in the menu to the parameters separated by underscores. The prefix, suffix, and name can also be set using the following lines in the control program: 

      set MC(<megacell>,prefix) <prefix> 
set MC(<megacell>,suffix) <suffix>
set MC(<megacell>,name) <name> 
     

For example: 

      set MC(sram,prefix) IU_
set MC(sram,suffix) {_$ROWS}
set MC(sram,name) ASNYC_RAM128X10 
     

Note that if you have multiple parameters, you need to be careful of the tcl syntax. (For more information on tcl, refer to the Scriptics tcl/tk page at http://www.scriptics.com.)

For example, if you have ROWS and COLUMNS as parameters and you want a suffix of the form 32X10, you need the line: 

      set MC(sram,suffix) {${ROWS}X$COLUMNS} 
     

The outside set of braces ({}) tells tcl to delay the evaluation of the variables. The inside set of braces ({}) tells tcl that the variable is ROWS, not ROWSX. The inside braces ({}) are also needed if an underscore (_) replaces the X.

MC Netlist

The MC Netlist command creates either a SPICE or Verilog netlist for the current MAX cell, as shown in Figure 3. The created netlists are "two-level"; that is, they have a main cell that calls leaf cells. In the case of SPICE, the leaf cells are extracted SPICE subckt's (subcircuits). In Verilog, they are hand built behavioral Verilog modules. For more information, see Netlisting .

    Figure 3: MC Netlist Popup Form 
     

You use the MC Netlist command to set the type of netlist and optionally include parasitics and comments (verbose mode). If you are creating a SPICE netlist for LVS, you typically do not want parasitics, but you do want them for simulation. Note that Verilog netlisting ignores the parasitics switch. The verbose mode adds comments to the netlist detailing which text labels in the layout are attached to which nets. This is useful for debugging, but makes the netlists very large.

MC Critical Path

The MC Critical Path command creates a SPICE netlist of the circuits in the cone of logic emanating in both directions from the selected cell(s). To run, you typically select the memory cell (for a memory) that is furthest away from the address/control inputs and then run MC Critical Path. This will bring up the pop-up menu shown in Figure 4.

    Figure 4: Critical Path Extraction Pop-up Menu 
     

It will either create a SPICE netlist of the critical path, create a layout cell containing only the polygons associated with the critical path, or simply bring up the critical path pop-up menu shown in Figure 5. If you select netlist, MCC will automatically create a small critical path netlist of the design (typically about 1000 devices) that can be simulated to verify performance from an extracted layout. The SPICE netlist includes R's and C's. For further details, see Critical Path Netlist .

    Figure 5: MC Critical Path Popup Form 
     

Once the critical path has been created, the menu in Figure 5 appears, allowing you to view the critical path. Once the path(s) has been simulated, the results can be plotted with the NST waveform viewer, as shown in Figure 6. For more information, see Extracting the Critical Path .

    Figure 6: Plotting Critical Path With NST Waveform Viewer 
     

MC What

The MC What command helps you to create the tiling programs for megacells. You do not need to run MC What, but it can help in creating tiling programs or converting megacells built by hand or by other tools into an MCC parameterized megacell.

The syntax for the tiler takes a little getting used to because of its lists-of-lists structure. MC What allows you to simply drop the instances in a layout the way you want them, and MC What will create the appropriate tiling commands to generate that layout (for more information, see the section Tiling ). The tiling commands are described in detail in Chapter 3, "Creating Megacells". Note that MC What only helps generate the tiling, it does not help set up via programming or port propagation.

    Figure 7: MC What Popup Form 
     

When you run MC What, you get a popup with three options as shown in Figure 7. By default, MC What only creates the MACRO line (refer to the section Tiling) for the current MAX cell and does not descend the hierarchy. If you turn on hierarchy, MC What will attempt to create the tiling commands for that cell all the way down to leaf cells. Thus if you run MC What on an entire hierarchical memory, you get a complete tiling program for that memory, if everything works correctly. MC What fails if the memory is not partitioned correctly or it cannot determine which cells are leaf cells.

The final two fields in the MC What menu are remove_prefix and remove_suffix. These act like the prefix and suffix fields in the MC Build command except in reverse. If you have a megacell that you are trying to decompose, these fields allow you to strip off prefixes or suffixes from all hierarchical cells.

Note that MC What does not necessarily create the best way to build a megacell; you might be able to group items more efficiently. Note also that MC What does not know when to add "TOP" or any other special keywords, and that in this version MC What ignores any spaces between abutment boundaries of cells.
